title: 6 Habits That Quietly Harm Your Career, And How to Shift Them -to-shift-them/
author: Nimish Lad
summary: Nimish Lad, writing on The Researcher Teacher, argues that most professional derailments stem not from a lack of talent but from small, often unconscious habits that erode growth gradually, like 'water eroding rock.' Drawing on his own career and observations of colleagues in schools and academic settings, he identifies six such habits and pairs each with a concrete reframe rather than a vague exhortation to change: dodging difficult conversations (reframed as expressing them through empathy - 'I want to bring this up because I value our working relationship'), downplaying one's own contributions (countered by keeping a running record of impact to draw on when it matters), perfectionism masquerading as high standards (reframed by adopting a 'working draft' mindset that values progress over polish), reflexively saying yes to avoid disappointing others (countered by deliberately buying time before committing), clinging to familiar routines out of comfort (reframed as embracing change as a low-stakes experiment), and avoiding self-promotion out of fear of seeming 'too much' (reframed as storytelling rather than boasting). His closing argument situates all six within a broader philosophy of professional growth: careers are built through accumulated daily choices rather than dramatic leaps, and the necessary first step for any of the six shifts is simple awareness that the habit exists.
points: Lad's foundational claim, opening with Aristotle: most professional derailments come not from lack of talent but from small, often unconscious habits that erode growth gradually - 'like water eroding rock.'

His fix for dodging difficult conversations is a specific empathetic framing phrase - 'I want to bring this up because I value our working relationship' - reframing directness as an act of care rather than confrontation.
His fix for perfectionism is the 'working draft' mindset, explicitly modelled for students as well as colleagues, valuing progress over polish and reducing the paralysis perfectionism induces.

His fix for reflexive over-commitment ('saying yes when you mean I'm overwhelmed') is a specific delaying phrase - 'Let me check my schedule and get back to you' - that buys time to genuinely assess capacity before agreeing.
His closing philosophy: careers 'are not built in giant leaps but in daily choices,' and for each of the six habits, the necessary first step is simple awareness that the pattern exists.
quotes: Throughout my career, I've observed that most professional derailments don't come from lack of talent, they come from habits. Often unconscious, they chip away at our growth slowly, like water eroding rock.
Silence may feel like safety, but avoidance breeds resentment. Whether it's a colleague who crossed a line, or a student who needs honest feedback, evading tough talks only magnifies issues.
Perfectionism is often celebrated, but in truth, it's fear in a polished coat. It tells us not to start unless it's flawless, and not to finish if it isn't.
In our drive to please, many of us say yes far too often, to extra tasks, favours, or responsibilities that don't align with our goals.
The fear of being "too much" can lead us to become too quiet. Yet, sharing our achievements is not arrogance, it's awareness.
Careers are not built in giant leaps but in daily choices. As with teaching and research, the goal isn't perfection, it's progress.
